text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Picture the person in charge of the supply chain at a company like a global sportswear brand or a big pharmaceutical group. Factories on three continents, thousands of suppliers, ships that may or may not arrive on time. And on Monday morning the chief executive asks a simple question. Are we better or worse at this than our rivals?

speaker: JAMES
text: And the honest answer, very often, is that nobody really knows. Your own numbers are inside your company. Your competitors' numbers are inside theirs. Consultants will happily sell you an opinion, but a real, current comparison with your peers is surprisingly hard to get.

speaker: NORA
text: So imagine a business whose whole job is to answer that kind of question. To gather the people who run supply chains, collect their data, compare it, and turn it into guidance. And then imagine that business arrives just as AI promises to answer questions instantly, for almost nothing.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the tension at the heart of today's episode.

speaker: NORA
text: Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills, which we'll often just call LLCP. Today it's Zero100, a young, London-based research and membership company for the people who run supply chains and operations at very large companies.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: company announcements, the private equity firm's pages, trade press and a few public databases. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a number or a claim comes from the company itself, we'll flag that. And nothing here is investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'll add a second warning up front. Zero100 is a private company that discloses very little. No revenue, no member count, no published prices. So today there will be more "we don't know" than usual, and I'd rather say that plainly than fill the gaps with guesses.

speaker: NORA
text: Good. So, James, the one-sentence version. What is Zero100?

speaker: JAMES
text: Zero100 sells paid memberships to chief supply chain officers, chief operating officers and their teams. Members get research, community benchmarks, which means data comparing their company with peers, and access to a network of other senior operations executives, through events and guidance.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three reasons. It's new, founded in 2021, so it was built in the AI era rather than adapting to it. It took a growth investment from LLCP announced in January 2025. And it describes its own research as, in its words, continuous AI-native analysis. So the question for this episode is whether that AI claim is a real engine or mostly a label, and what it would take to make it the engine.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. Where is Zero100 and who runs it?
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: JAMES
text: It's headquartered in London, and an announcement from 2022 also mentions a New York office. The legal entity, according to a deal database, is Zero100 Community Limited, although the footer on its own website reads Z100 Community Limited. Small thing, but it tells you this is a young company still tidying its identity.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: NORA
text: And the people?
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: JAMES
text: The chief executive is Olly Sloboda, who is described as a co-founder. The founder and chief research officer is O'Marah, who has a long public profile in supply chain research. A 2022 announcement described him as co-founder, and a business database lists him as founder, so the exact founding story is a little blurry. That same 2022 announcement also named Deborah Dull as a senior research director.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: NORA
text: So a research-led leadership team.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much. And that matters because in a business like this, the people who write the research are a big part of what members are buying. We'll come back to that as a risk.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: NORA
text: How big is it?
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: JAMES
text: When LLCP announced its investment in January 2025, it said Zero100 had more than fifty employees. That's the only size figure we found. Revenue isn't public. The number of members isn't public. What is public is a list of clients that LLCP itself names: Nike, Walmart, Unilever, Pfizer, Google, Honeywell and Volvo Cars, among others.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: NORA
text: That's a serious list for a company that's only a few years old.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. Those are some of the most complex supply chains on the planet: sportswear, retail, consumer goods, pharmaceuticals, technology, industrial products, cars. And it tells you the buyer is very senior. These aren't companies buying a cheap newsletter. They're buying access for their top operations people.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: NORA
text: Tell me about the early years.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: JAMES
text: The company was founded in 2021. In January 2022 it announced the founding members of its advisory board, roughly fourteen chief supply chain and operations executives at launch. That's a classic move for a community business. Before you have a big membership, you recruit a group of respected names who lend credibility and help shape the agenda.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: NORA
text: It's a bit like a new club getting a few famous people to join first.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly that. If the head of supply chain at a household-name company is on your board, the next one is more likely to take your call. And in its early years Zero100 also ran events. One example we found from 2024: Estée Lauder and Zero100 convened about forty leaders in New York. And its podcast has an episode titled Zero100 Live 2024: AI Takes The Mainstage, which tells you AI was a theme of its flagship event that year.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: NORA
text: So by 2024 it had a board, a client list, events and a podcast.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: JAMES
text: And a positioning around AI and digital transformation. Its careers page talks about helping to, quote, unlock the true potential of the AI and Digital Revolution. So AI has been part of the pitch from early on.
chapter: Who Zero100 is and how it started

speaker: NORA
text: Now the private equity part. How did LLCP get involved?

speaker: JAMES
text: On the ninth of January 2025, LLCP announced a growth investment in Zero100. The terms weren't disclosed. No seller was named, and the founders and existing management continued alongside LLCP. A month later, the law firm Hogan Lovells said it had advised the founders and management on the deal, and that the investment would strengthen technology, data, research and talent and support new products and services.

speaker: NORA
text: "Growth investment" is a phrase that can mean a lot of things. What does it usually mean?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, and this is background rather than anything specific to this deal, a growth investment usually means the investor puts capital into a company that's already working, often a founder-led one, to help it scale, rather than buying it outright with a lot of debt. Here we don't know the stake size, so I won't guess whether LLCP holds a majority or a minority.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned a date conflict.

speaker: JAMES
text: A small one. LLCP's portfolio page lists the investment date as December 2024, while the press release, the law firm and a deal database all point to the January 2025 announcement. The likeliest explanation, and it's only our guess, is that the deal closed in December and was announced in January. Either way, as of November 2026 LLCP has been involved for a little under two years.

speaker: NORA
text: What did LLCP say about why it invested?

speaker: JAMES
text: LLCP's Josh Kaufman said Zero100 is, quote, uniquely positioned to support clients on board-level supply chain objectives. And the chief executive, Olly Sloboda, said the partnership would help pursue its vision of transforming the supply chain intelligence market. "Supply chain intelligence market" is an interesting phrase. It frames Zero100 not as an events company or a consultancy, but as an intelligence business.

speaker: NORA
text: Any acquisitions since?

speaker: JAMES
text: None that we found. That's worth noting, because a lot of companies in this portfolio grow by buying other businesses. Zero100, so far, appears to be growing on its own.

speaker: NORA
text: And any recognition?

speaker: JAMES
text: In May 2026 a logistics trade site ran a headline saying Zero100 had won a King's Award for Enterprise. That's a UK honour for businesses. But we only saw the headline, we couldn't open the article, and we couldn't confirm which category it was in. So, a positive signal, with an asterisk.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's get to the customer. What's actually hard about being a chief supply chain officer?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's one of those jobs that went from back office to front page in a few years. When supply chains work, nobody notices. When they break, it's on the news. Think about the last several years in general: a pandemic, shipping disruption, shortages, tariffs, pressure to cut emissions. All of that lands on the supply chain leader's desk.

speaker: NORA
text: And the board starts asking questions.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. And they're hard questions. How resilient are we? What would happen if this supplier failed? Are our inventory levels sensible compared with others in our industry? Should we be spending more on automation, or on AI? How do we find and train people for jobs that didn't exist five years ago? A trade headline we found talks about an AI talent dash in supply chain, with companies scrambling to upskill staff.

speaker: NORA
text: So where does a supply chain leader go for answers today?

speaker: JAMES
text: A few places, in general. Their own teams and data, which only tell them about themselves. Big consultancies, which are expensive and project-based. Analyst firms, which publish research and run benchmarks. Software vendors, who have a point of view but also something to sell. And their peers, which is often the most valuable source and the hardest to access in a structured way.

speaker: NORA
text: Peers being other people doing the same job at other companies.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. The head of supply chain at a consumer goods company would love to know how her counterpart at another consumer goods company handled a port closure, or how they structured their planning team. Those conversations happen at conferences, over dinner, through personal networks. But they're informal, patchy and hard to turn into numbers.

speaker: NORA
text: And Zero100's pitch is to make that structured.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's how I'd put it. It combines three things. A peer network, so leaders can meet and talk. Community benchmarks, so the network's data can be compared. And research, so analysts can turn that data and those conversations into guidance. The homepage promises, quote, personalized insights in days, not quarters. And it describes its guidance as operator-led and driven by AI.

speaker: NORA
text: "Days, not quarters." That's a speed claim.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a direct shot at traditional research, where a big report might take months to produce. And it's exactly where AI should help, because the slow part of research is gathering, cleaning and writing, which is analyst time.

speaker: NORA
text: You said the buyer is senior. Who actually signs the cheque?

speaker: JAMES
text: We don't have direct evidence, but our inference from the client list is that a chief supply chain officer or COO buys it from an enterprise budget, much like other executive memberships. And there's a second type of buyer. In February 2025, Körber Supply Chain Software, a supply chain software vendor, announced that it had joined the Zero100 community. A trade headline also says Puma joined, though we couldn't confirm the date. So the community includes both big operating companies and vendors who sell to them.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go deeper on what a member actually gets. Walk me through it.

speaker: JAMES
text: With a caveat that Zero100 doesn't publish a full menu or prices, here's what the public material describes. First, research. Zero100 publishes analysis on supply chain and operations topics, and its homepage highlights AI and transformation strategy as a theme. Second, surveys and benchmarks. For example, it promotes a State of the COO 2026 survey of one hundred operations leaders. Third, the community and events. Its homepage mentions events in places like Phoenix, San Diego and Dublin, on top of its London and New York base. And fourth, guidance, which sounds like more personalised advice for members.

speaker: NORA
text: A survey of a hundred people. Is that a lot?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's modest in statistical terms, but in this world it can be valuable, because it's a hundred very senior people. A survey of a hundred chief operating officers can tell you things a survey of ten thousand random workers can't. The trick is being honest about what a sample that size can and can't support.

speaker: NORA
text: And the benchmarks. What are they, in plain terms?

speaker: JAMES
text: A benchmark is a comparison. Say a member wants to know whether their planning team is the right size for a company of their revenue and complexity. If enough members share how they're structured, the research team can show the range: here's the typical size, here's the spread, here's where you sit. Zero100 describes these as community benchmarks, which suggests the data comes from members themselves.

speaker: NORA
text: Which is a nice loop. Members give data and get insight back.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a powerful loop when it works. The more members, the better the benchmarks. The better the benchmarks, the more valuable membership is. Economists call that a network effect. But it only works if members trust that their data is handled carefully, and if enough of them actually contribute.

speaker: NORA
text: And the events?

speaker: JAMES
text: Events do two jobs. They're part of the value, because senior people want to meet peers. And they're a sales engine, because a great event is how you persuade the next company to join. The Estée Lauder gathering of about forty leaders is a good example of the format: a member company hosts, Zero100 convenes, and peers spend a day on shared problems.

speaker: NORA
text: So if I had to describe the product, it's part research firm, part club, part data business.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a very good summary. And the balance between those three matters a lot for the AI story. A club is hard to automate. Research is easier to speed up. A data business is where AI can really multiply value.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make this concrete. Invent a member for me. Not a real person or company.

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Let's call her Priya. She's the chief supply chain officer at a made-up mid-sized consumer goods company. They make household products, sell through big retailers, and have factories in two countries and a lot of contract manufacturers. She has a team of several hundred people and a chief executive who has just come back from a board meeting with three questions.

speaker: NORA
text: What are the three questions?

speaker: JAMES
text: One: our inventory has crept up, is that normal for our industry right now? Two: our competitors are talking about AI in planning, are we behind? Three: we're struggling to hire planners, what are others doing about it?

speaker: NORA
text: And without something like Zero100?

speaker: JAMES
text: Priya asks her team for an internal analysis, which tells her about her own company. She calls two or three peers she knows, who are friendly but busy. She might commission a consultancy, which takes weeks and costs real money. Or she reads analyst reports that are useful but not specific to her situation. She ends up giving the board a thoughtful answer built mostly on her own judgment.

speaker: NORA
text: And with a membership?

speaker: JAMES
text: In the model Zero100 describes, she can go to its research and benchmarks first. She looks at what the community data says about inventory trends in consumer goods. She reads its work on AI in planning, which is the kind of topic its homepage highlights. She asks the Zero100 team for a personalised view, which is the "days, not quarters" promise. And at the next event she sits at a table with three other chief supply chain officers who have the same planner shortage, and hears what's actually working.

speaker: NORA
text: So she walks into the next board meeting with comparisons, not just opinions.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the value. "Here's where we sit relative to peers, here's what leaders in our industry are doing, here's my recommendation." For a senior executive, that's career-relevant. It makes her look prepared and makes her decisions more defensible.

speaker: NORA
text: And where does it fall short in that story, today?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, the bottleneck is the personalised piece. If Priya's question needs an analyst to dig through data and write a tailored answer, that takes analyst time. If fifty members ask similar questions in the same week, the research team becomes the constraint. Which is exactly where an AI research assistant could change the economics, and we'll come back to that.

speaker: NORA
text: And I suppose the community piece doesn't scale in the same way either.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. You can't automate the dinner where Priya meets her peers. But you can make sure that when she gets back to her desk, the follow-up data and research are waiting for her, rather than in a queue.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk market. How big is the market for supply chain research and executive networks?
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a reliable figure, so we're not going to give one. It's part of a broader world of business research, advisory and executive networks, which is large in general, but carving out the supply chain slice with a number we trust wasn't possible from public sources.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: Fair. Who does Zero100 compete with?
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: Our research here was thinner than usual, so I'll separate what's sourced from what's general knowledge. Sourced: a business database page compares Zero100 with Manhattan Associates, which is a supply chain software company. But that's a comparison page, not a competitor list, and Manhattan sells software, not peer networks. Körber, as we said, is a member, not a rival.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: And the general knowledge?
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: Speaking generally and cautiously, the obvious large competitor for this kind of business is Gartner, the big research and advisory firm, which publishes supply chain research and runs executive programmes and peer communities. Then there are the large consultancies, which produce benchmarks and thought leadership partly to win consulting work. There are other analyst firms. And there are executive membership organisations in general. We didn't find a sourced list of direct peer-network rivals, so I won't name specific ones.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: So Zero100 is a young company competing, in part, with some very big and established names.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. And that's both a challenge and an opportunity. Big incumbents have scale, brand and huge research libraries. A young company can move faster, focus tightly on one executive role, and build its research process around AI from the start rather than retrofitting it. That's the theory, at least.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: What about vendors?
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a really interesting dynamic. Software vendors increasingly want access to buyer communities, so they join or sponsor them, like Körber did. But vendors also run their own user groups and customer communities. If the big software companies build strong communities of their own, an independent network has to offer something they can't, which is neutrality. A chief supply chain officer trusts a peer comparison more if it isn't run by someone selling her software.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: So neutrality is a selling point that also limits how much you can lean on vendor money.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a good way of putting it. Vendor members are useful revenue, but if the community starts to feel like a sales channel, the executives may drift away. Getting that balance right is one of the key judgments in this business.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: I want to spend a few minutes on how research businesses make money, because I think it explains the AI opportunity.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: Agreed. In general terms, research and membership businesses tend to sell subscriptions. A company pays a yearly fee for access, often for a set number of people, sometimes with extra fees for events, advisory time or custom work. Zero100 doesn't publish prices, so I'm describing the category, not its actual terms.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: And the costs?
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: Mostly people. Analysts who research and write, community managers who organise events and look after members, and sales staff who bring in new members. In a business with more than fifty employees whose main product is research and guidance, our inference is that analyst time is both the biggest cost and the biggest limit on growth.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: So if you want more members, you need more analysts.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: In the traditional model, roughly, yes. Each new member brings more questions, more requests for tailored work, more expectations of attention. That makes research firms grow in a fairly straight line: revenue and headcount rising together. That's fine, but it's not the kind of growth investors get most excited about.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: And the other thing that matters is retention.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: Huge. A subscription business lives or dies on renewals. If members renew year after year, each new member adds to a growing base. If they drift away after a year, you're constantly refilling a leaky bucket. And what drives renewal in executive memberships, in general, is perceived value: did I use it, did it help me, did my boss notice?
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: Which comes back to Priya walking into the board meeting prepared.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Every time a member gets a useful answer quickly, renewal gets more likely. Every time they forget they even have the membership, it gets less likely.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: So where does AI fit into these economics?
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: In two places. On the cost side, AI can make each analyst far more productive: finding data, drafting analysis, summarising what members are saying. That breaks the straight line between headcount and revenue. On the value side, AI can let members get answers themselves, at any time, which increases how often they use the membership. More usage, in general, means better renewal. Both of those are inferences, but they're the logic of the opportunity.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: And the danger, of course, is that AI does the same thing for everyone else.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the threat in a nutshell. If a general AI tool can answer a decent share of benchmark-style questions for free, a paid research product has to be clearly better. Which, in my view, means it has to rest on data the free tools don't have.
chapter: The market, competitors and the economics of research

speaker: NORA
text: Okay, the reality check. Where is Zero100 actually with AI? Strip out the marketing.

speaker: JAMES
text: Here's what we found. The homepage positions the company around, quote, continuous AI-native analysis and operator-led guidance driven by AI. The careers page talks about the AI and digital revolution. AI and transformation strategy is a headline research theme. The 2024 flagship event was themed around AI. And the LLCP investment was said to support new products and services.

speaker: NORA
text: And what didn't you find?

speaker: JAMES
text: No named AI product. No AI partnership. No AI acquisition. No public AI hires. The careers page we looked at listed open roles in central functions, communications and operations, with nothing that was clearly AI or data science. And the "AI-native analysis" claim isn't tied to any described step in how the research is actually produced.

speaker: NORA
text: So, in plain terms?

speaker: JAMES
text: In plain terms, from the outside, AI at Zero100 today is mostly a topic and a promise. It's a topic, because Zero100 researches and advises on AI for supply chain leaders, and that's genuinely valuable. And it's a promise, because the company says its own analysis is AI-native. What's missing in public is evidence of AI as a product members can touch.

speaker: NORA
text: Is that unfair? It might be doing a lot behind the scenes.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's quite possible. Plenty of research firms use AI internally to speed up their analysts without announcing it. I want to be clear that absence of public evidence isn't evidence of absence. But for a company that leads with AI in its positioning, I'd expect a buyer, or a future acquirer, to ask to see it working.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the data side? That seems important.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's the strongest part of the story. Community benchmarks and member survey data are a real, proprietary data asset. Nobody else has exactly that data about exactly those companies. That's the raw material for any serious AI product.

speaker: NORA
text: And governance? Security?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a public security certification or an AI policy. To be fair, we didn't get to check thoroughly for the common British and international security standards, so I'd call it not found rather than absent. But it matters a lot here. If members are sharing operational data about Nike-scale supply chains, they'll want to know exactly how it's stored, who sees it and whether it's ever used to train AI models.

speaker: NORA
text: So the overall read?

speaker: JAMES
text: Strong positioning, a valuable data asset, a real expert team, and a gap between saying AI-native and showing it. The good news is that the gap is closable, and the investment was explicitly meant to fund technology and data.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's be specific about the challenges. What do you think keeps Zero100's leadership up at night?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, scale. More than fifty employees is still small, and it's competing for the attention of executives who are approached by everyone. Every year it has to prove it deserves a place in their calendar and their budget.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, the research model itself is under pressure from AI. If a supply chain leader can ask a general AI assistant to summarise trends in inventory management, some of the value of a written research report gets squeezed. That doesn't kill the business, but it raises the bar. Research has to be more specific, more data-driven and more personal to justify a premium.

speaker: NORA
text: Third.

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, proving the AI claim. As we said, the positioning is ahead of the visible product. In the short term that's fine. In the long term, when the next investor or buyer does diligence, they'll ask what AI product exists, how many members use it and what it does to retention.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth.

speaker: JAMES
text: Key people. In research businesses, members often follow particular experts. If a small number of research leaders carry the brand, losing one is a real risk. Building a bench, and building systems that capture the firm's knowledge rather than leaving it in people's heads, is important. Interestingly, AI can help with that too.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Transparency. Zero100 publishes no pricing and no member numbers. For a private company that's normal, and I'm not criticising it for that. But it means outsiders, including potential members, can't easily judge value. Our inference is that sales depends heavily on reputation and word of mouth, which works well in a tight executive community, but has limits as you try to grow into new regions and segments.

speaker: NORA
text: There's also the small brand thing you mentioned.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, Zero100 versus Z100 Community Limited. Minor, but in a world where people search for you, consistency helps. It's an easy fix.

speaker: NORA
text: And the time question for the owners.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. LLCP has been involved for under two years. We don't know its intended holding period. But in general, private equity investors want to see a value creation plan show results within the first few years. So there's a natural push to move from promise to evidence fairly quickly.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's move to opportunities. If you were on Zero100's board, where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: The biggest one, in my view, is an AI research assistant built on Zero100's own research, benchmarks and survey data, offered to members as a self-serve product. Members ask questions in plain language and get answers grounded in the community's data, with the sources shown. We'll spend a chapter on that.

speaker: NORA
text: What else?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, turning benchmarks into a product of their own. Today benchmarks seem to be part of the research and events. They could become subscription data feeds or dashboards, where a member can see where they sit against peers at any time. That moves value from one-off moments to something members use every week.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pricing tiers. If there's currently one main membership, there's room for options between event-only access and full advisory membership, perhaps with usage-based access to benchmarks or the assistant. That lets Zero100 sell to more of each member company: not just the chief supply chain officer, but the planning director, the procurement lead and so on. All of this is our inference, because we don't know today's structure.

speaker: NORA
text: And vendors?

speaker: JAMES
text: A formal sponsor programme for vendors is a natural step. Körber already joined. A structured tier, with clear rules on what vendors get and don't get, could bring in revenue while protecting neutrality.

speaker: NORA
text: Geography?

speaker: JAMES
text: Zero100 already has events in the United States and Europe, in places like Phoenix, San Diego and Dublin, on top of London and New York. Expanding to the Asia-Pacific region and to the American mid-market, meaning operations leaders at companies smaller than the giants on the client list, are both plausible. An AI assistant makes that more affordable, because you can serve more members without a matching rise in analysts.

speaker: NORA
text: And acquisitions?

speaker: JAMES
text: None so far. But a tuck-in of a survey or benchmarking data business would widen the data asset, which feeds the AI opportunity. That's our view of a sensible target, not anything the company has said.

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned talent earlier, the scramble to upskill. Is there an opportunity there?

speaker: JAMES
text: I think there's a real one, although it's our inference rather than anything Zero100 has announced. If supply chain teams need to learn new skills, especially around AI and data, then a trusted community for those leaders is a natural place to offer learning. Short programmes for planners and analysts, peer cohorts for new managers, briefings for leaders on what AI can and can't do in operations.

speaker: NORA
text: That would widen the audience beyond the top executive.

speaker: JAMES
text: It would. Today the visible buyer is the chief supply chain officer. Learning products could reach the hundreds of people who work for her. And that has a nice side effect. When a whole team uses the membership, not just one person, it becomes much harder to cancel.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a danger of spreading too thin?

speaker: JAMES
text: Definitely. A company of fifty-odd people can't do everything at once. If I had to rank these, I'd put the AI research assistant and benchmark products first, because they build on the core data asset. Pricing tiers and vendor sponsorship next, because they're mostly commercial design. Learning and geography after that. And acquisitions only when there's a clear data business that fits.

speaker: NORA
text: And cross-selling advisory work?

speaker: JAMES
text: Possibly. Members who trust the research may want help putting it into practice, for example on digital transformation. The care point is that advisory work is people-heavy, so it can pull the company back towards the straight-line growth model. I'd treat it as a complement, not the core.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI bet for the next eighteen months, what is it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: The member research assistant. It plays directly to the strongest asset, the proprietary community data and research. It speeds up the "days, not quarters" promise towards minutes. It reduces pressure on analysts. And it gives members a reason to use their membership every week, which should help renewal. I want to be clear that we haven't seen any numbers on hours saved or revenue, so the size of the prize is unknown. But the logic is strong.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: How is that different from just using a general chatbot?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Three ways. The data: it would answer from Zero100's benchmarks and member surveys, which no general tool has. The context: it would know the member's industry and size, so answers are relevant. And the trust: it would show where each answer comes from, and flag when the data is thin. A general tool might give a confident answer with no basis. A good research assistant should say, here's what our community data shows, here's the sample, and here's where you should talk to an analyst.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: So how would you run it? Give me the first hundred days.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: get the foundations in order. Inventory all the research, benchmarks and survey data. Decide what can be used and under what permissions, because members gave that data on certain terms. Write a clear data and AI policy for members. And pick a small group of design partner members, perhaps eight to ten, who are keen and will give honest feedback.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Build an internal version first. Give Zero100's own analysts the assistant and let them use it to answer real member questions, checking every answer before it goes out. That does two things. It speeds up the analysts straight away. And it shows where the assistant is wrong, which you want to find out in private, not in front of a chief supply chain officer at a household-name company.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: The shadow mode idea again.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Then days sixty to a hundred: open it to the design partner members, with clear labelling, sources on every answer and an easy route to a human analyst. Measure three things: how often they use it, how fast they get answers compared with before, and how they rate the answers. At day one hundred, decide on wider rollout and on how to price it, based on evidence.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Who owns it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: One person, ideally a product leader who understands both research and technology. Right now the public leadership is research-led, so this may mean a new hire. And they need the chief research officer's backing, because the research team's trust in the tool is what makes it credible to members.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Let's replay Priya's board questions with the assistant in place. Still hypothetical.

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. It's Monday afternoon. Priya opens the Zero100 member portal and types: how have inventory levels moved for consumer goods companies of our size over the past year, and what are leaders doing about it?

speaker: NORA
text: And what comes back?

speaker: JAMES
text: In the version I'd want, the assistant first checks what data it has. It says something like: our community benchmark includes a certain number of consumer goods companies in your size range, here's the median and the range, and here's where your company sits based on the data you shared. Then it pulls from recent research: three themes leaders are pursuing, with links to the underlying analysis. And then it adds a note: the sample for your exact segment is small, so treat this as directional, and here's an analyst you can book for thirty minutes.

speaker: NORA
text: I like that last part. It's honest about its limits.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's essential. In executive research, being wrong in front of a board is the worst outcome. An assistant that's confident and wrong would damage trust in the whole membership. One that's careful and quick builds it.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the AI question? "Are we behind on AI in planning?"

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a great one, because it's Zero100's home topic. The assistant could draw on the State of the COO survey, for example what share of operations leaders report using AI in planning, and on case material from the community. Then it might suggest which peers in the network have spoken publicly about their approach, and which upcoming event covers it.

speaker: NORA
text: So the assistant becomes a front door to the community, not just to documents.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the bigger idea. The best version doesn't replace the people part of the membership, it routes members into it more effectively. Ask a question, get the data, and get introduced to the right peer or analyst.

speaker: NORA
text: And from Zero100's side, what does it learn?

speaker: JAMES
text: A lot. Every question members ask is a signal of what they care about. If two hundred members ask about planner shortages in a month, that's the next research report and the next event theme. So the assistant also becomes a sensor for the research agenda. Of course, those questions are sensitive too, so they need the same careful data handling.

speaker: NORA
text: And the planner shortage question?

speaker: JAMES
text: That one is probably best answered by the community itself. The assistant might summarise what research exists, then say: twelve members have flagged this as a priority, would you like to join a small working group? That turns a question into a reason to engage more deeply, and that, in my view, is what drives renewal.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other businesses learn from Zero100?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd pull out four lessons. First, if you sell expertise, your data is your defence against AI. General AI tools are trained on public information. Anything you know that's not public, your members' benchmarks, your surveys, your case history, is what lets you stay ahead. Businesses selling knowledge should ask: what do we know that nobody else does?

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, make sure the AI claim and the AI product are on the same timeline. Saying AI-native on your homepage is easy. Every competitor will say it soon. The winners will be the ones who can show a member a working tool. If your positioning is ahead of your product, close the gap before a buyer, a customer or a competitor points it out.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, use AI to scale people, not replace them. In a community business, the human relationships are the product. The smart move is to let AI handle the searching, summarising and drafting, so that the experts and community managers spend more time with members. That's true of a lot of professional services, from law to accountancy to consulting.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, trust is a feature. When customers share data with you, how you handle it is part of what they're buying. A clear, published policy on data and AI, and the security credentials to back it up, can win business. It's especially true when your customers are big, cautious companies with lawyers who read the fine print.

speaker: NORA
text: I'd add one from the Priya story. Think about what makes your customer look good to their boss.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a great addition. Executive products succeed when they make the buyer more effective in front of the people they report to. If your product helps your customer walk into a board meeting with answers, they'll fight to keep it in the budget.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a lesson here for investors too?

speaker: JAMES
text: I think so. When you invest in a business whose positioning includes AI, ask early what AI exists today, what's planned, and how you'll know it's working. Build the measures in from the start, so that by the time of any sale, the story is backed by evidence.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk risks. Give me the list.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, AI disruption of the research model. General tools answer more benchmark-style questions over time, and analyst-written content loses pricing power. Two, commoditised benchmarks. Consultancies and analyst firms often publish survey data cheaply or for free to win other business. Three, vendor-run communities crowding out independent ones. Four, dependence on a few key research leaders. And five, execution: building a credible AI product with a small team, while running events and research at the same time.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a data risk?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. If the company builds an AI assistant on member data and gets the permissions or security wrong, that's a serious trust problem. In a tight community of senior executives, news like that travels fast. So I'd put data governance not just under risks, but at the start of any AI plan.

speaker: NORA
text: Walk me through how that could go wrong, concretely.

speaker: JAMES
text: Imagine, hypothetically, a member asks the assistant a question about inventory benchmarks, and the answer is so specific that another member's data can be worked out from it. Say there are only three companies in a segment, and the assistant shows the average. Two of them could, in principle, work out the third. That's a known problem in benchmarking in general, and it gets easier to trip over when an AI is generating answers on the fly.

speaker: NORA
text: So how do you prevent it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Standard techniques exist. Minimum group sizes, so you never show a figure built from fewer than a set number of companies. Rounding and ranges instead of exact numbers. Clear rules on what the assistant is allowed to reveal. And testing, where your own team deliberately tries to make the assistant leak information before any member sees it. None of this is exotic, but it has to be designed in from day one.

speaker: NORA
text: And the other side of governance, the question of whether member data trains AI models.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the question every big company's lawyers will ask. The cleanest answer, in my view, is that member data is used to answer member questions within Zero100's own system, under clear terms, and is not used to train outside models. Whatever the answer is, it should be written down, published and easy to explain.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owners?

speaker: JAMES
text: Timing and proof. A growth investment is a bet that the company can scale. The proof points a future investor or buyer would look for, in our view, are growth in members, strong renewal, more revenue per member, and a product, AI or otherwise, that makes the business less dependent on adding analysts for every new client.

speaker: NORA
text: So what should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four things. First, whether Zero100 launches a named AI product for members, and whether it publishes any usage numbers. Second, any confirmed detail on the King's Award, which would be a nice validation. Third, whether it makes its first acquisition, and whether that's a data business. And fourth, whether it publishes a data and AI policy for members, which would signal it's taking the trust side seriously.

speaker: NORA
text: And if none of those happen?

speaker: JAMES
text: Then the company may still be growing well, but quietly. Private companies don't owe the public updates. But for one that leads with AI, I'd expect to see evidence surface within the next year or so.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: Is Zero100 an events company?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. Events are part of it. It's a research, benchmark and peer network business.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Its community data and the trust of very senior members.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: Small and opaque. No public numbers, and an AI claim ahead of a visible AI product.

speaker: NORA
text: Best evidence of momentum?

speaker: JAMES
text: A client list that includes Nike, Walmart, Unilever and Pfizer, by LLCP's account.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: A member research assistant built on its own benchmarks and surveys.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI kill paid research?

speaker: JAMES
text: It'll kill generic paid research. Research built on data nobody else has gets more valuable.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a chief supply chain officer should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Ask yourself which of your big decisions are based on real peer comparisons, and which on gut feel. Then fix the most important gap.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cautious optimist. The ingredients are there. It needs to show the AI working.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. Zero100 is a London-based company founded in 2021 that sells memberships to the people who run supply chains and operations at very large companies, combining research, community benchmarks and an executive peer network. It has a blue-chip client list, more than fifty employees by the last public count, and a growth investment from LLCP announced in January 2025 to strengthen its technology, data, research and talent. It positions itself as AI-native, but from the outside AI is so far more a topic and a promise than a product members can touch. Its biggest opportunity is to turn its proprietary community data into an AI research assistant that gives members trustworthy answers in minutes and routes them into the community. The risks are AI eroding generic research, a small team carrying a lot, and the need to prove the claim with evidence.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the wider lesson is one we'll keep coming back to in this series. When AI makes general knowledge cheap, the valuable thing is knowledge that only you have, delivered in a way people trust.
